segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can identify this group of -go verbs and expect them to go to -ga when they are in the subjunctive, or the "mood" tense. So, "I leave" from salir is?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salgo. And if I want to tell somebody, "Leave!" formally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salga. And if I want to tell more than one person?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And if I want to tell them, "Don't leave!"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No salgan. Good. Poner was to put. "I put"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pongo. Good. Let's speak formally: "Put it here." "Put it here."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And where does that lo go with positive commands?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Póngalo aquí. But, "Don't put it here"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No lo ponga aquí. We saw with regular verbs that we have a shortcut where we don't use the "mood" tense for informal positive commands. So if I want to tell you to eat, I can just say, "Come." I go to comes and I drop the -s: "Come." If I want to tell you to find it, I can go to encontrar, encuentras, I can drop the -s: "Encuéntralo." That's our shortcut for informal positive commands where we don't use the "mood" tense. With this -go verbs, to make that shortcut you just drop the -go. Ah? So for example, how do you say, "I have" from tener?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo. If you want to tell somebody informally, "Have!", you just drop the -go.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For formal, but we're now looking at the shortcut that we have for informal. So how would you say, "Have it!" speaking formally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Téngalo. But informally we're not using the "mood" tense. We have a shortcut, it's just different to the shortcut we learned before. The shortcut is just dropping the -go: tenlo. A nice way to remember this is how you will see people in many Spanish-speaking countries answering the phone: either dígame, formally, or dime, informally. What is "I come"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And how do you tell somebody formally to come?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Venga. Now how would you make it informal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ven. Good. So I should mention that the venga that you hear in Spain as "come on!" is not necessarily formal. It's lost that feeling of formality because it's like a fixed expression. So ¡venga, venga! you hear all the time. And then ven will sound much more like "come", physically come, rather than "come on". ¡Venga, venga, venga! is used like "come on!". What was to leave, or to go out?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sal. We can just drop the -go. "I say" or "I tell" is digo. If you want to say, "Tell me" formally, how is it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dígame. If you want to make that same command informally, how will it be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dime. Good. So both things you hear when people answer the phone in Spain: dime, dígame, and in other countries, in other Spanish-speaking countries as well. So for -go verbs, they will go to -ga to form the "mood" tense, and for the orders, the shortcut for the informal positive order, they will just drop this -go. So, if you want to say, "Tell me when you come", speaking informally, how would that be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. After cuándo, we're using the "mood" tense because we're referring to the future: Dime cuándo vengas, "Tell me when you come." How would you say, "Tell me when you do it", and let's speak formally now: "Tell me when you do it", speaking formally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Dígame cuándo lo haga. Good.
